newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia firms plan lifting full Iraq oil entitlement.
newsitem.headline: Russia firms plan lifting full Iraq oil entitlement.

text.p: Russian oil firms still plan to lift their full entitlement of Iraqi crude oil under the United Nations oil-for-food agreement, a senior Russian oil executive said on Tuesday.

"Russian companies are carrying out purchases of Iraqi crude according to the contracts signed with the Iraqi state oil company SOMO," said Yuri Agababov, deputy director of Zarubezhneft, the company coordinating Russian purchases of Iraqi oil.

Seven Russian companies are contracted to lift a total of 25.2 million barrels, at 140,000 barrels a day (bpd) over six months from Iraq's outlets at Ceyhan on the Turkish Mediterranean and its Gulf port Mina al-Bakr.
But liftings by February 18 had totalled just 5.86 million barrels, said Zagababov, a rate of little more than 80,000 bpd since the six-month sale got underway on December 10.
Zagababov said that Zarubezhneft, LUKoil and Alfa-Eko completed their first liftings of Iraqi oil in January.

Scheduled liftings were made on February 4 by Zarubezhneft and LUKoil, Nafta-Moskva completed its first on February 7 and Alfa-Eko planned to make its next scheduled lifting of 1.8 million barrels on February 24, he said.
Iraq has been forced to make extra spot sales to make up for a revenue shortfall caused by falling oil prices in the past few weeks.
Traders said some of the Russian companies had found difficulty in reselling their crude, particularly since the slide in differentials for competitor grades.
Zagababov said there might be changes to the amount of Iraqi oil Russian companies intend to buy if Iraq succeeds in renewing the U.N. exchange for another six month period.
"As for the future, it's difficult to say, because it depends on the situation in the market.
"There may be changes (in volumes) of course...but that depends on Iraq's position."
Iraq began exporting oil in December 1996 for the first time in six years under a U.N. deal which allows Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of crude over six months to pay for food and medicine.
